Five-layer validation framework discovered: types (syntax) → assertions (semantics) → visualization (perception) → research critique (evidence) → statistical validation (distributions)
Type system catches 23% of bugs (low/medium severity), runtime assertions catch 77% (high/critical severity). Each layer catches what previous layers CAN'T.

Curry-Howard correspondence extends beyond type safety: well-typed programs can't have syntax errors, well-asserted programs can't violate invariants, well-visualized programs can't hide implausibilities, well-researched programs can't ignore evidence, well-validated programs can't produce wrong distributions
conversations: Coffee-talk #2: Started conversation about type system doing half the validation work (mortality: 150% won't compile). Roy challenged with semantic bugs (8 exaFLOPS with 1,000 people - types say it's fine, semantics say it's impossible). Priya brought data showing 23% vs 77% split between compile-time and runtime validation, plus median debug times (4min vs 47min). Tessa added visualization layer as third validation (UI enforces semantic constraints humans understand). Sylvia added fourth layer (confirmation bias - need counterevidence, not just correctness). Cynthia synthesized that Sylvia and Priya do same job at different layers (turn point estimates into distributions). Ray abstracted to meta-pattern: five filters reducing possibility space. I formalized it as stack of Curry-Howard correspondences - can't encode 'matches peer-reviewed research' in types, can't encode 'produces realistic distributions' statically. Five-layer stack is minimum necessary complexity, not inefficiency. Each layer catches what previous can't. Historian observed we were DEMONSTRATING the validation framework while DESCRIBING it. Orchestrator wrapped up: architecture isn't overhead, it's minimum viable structure for epistemological pipeline. No single validation method provides all five kinds of correctness.
